sections.title: What insurance is and its two families

blocks.text: **Insurance** is a contract in which an insurer promises to make good (indemnify) another party for losses caused by a specified risk or peril. Put differently, a company or the state guarantees compensation for a named loss, damage, illness or death, and in return the customer pays a fixed price called the **premium**.

blocks.title: Core terms
rows: The company or corporation that takes on the risk and pays the claim.
The person (or group) who buys the cover and pays the premium.
The price paid for the cover, as fixed by the policy terms.
Compensation that puts the insured back to the position before the loss.
The uncertain event (death, fire, accident, illness) that the policy protects against.

blocks.title: How an insurance contract works
items: Policy bought
Insurer and customer agree the terms
Premium paid
Customer pays the agreed price
Peril occurs
Death, fire, accident, illness...
Claim made
Customer or nominee informs insurer
Compensation
Insurer pays as per the policy

blocks.text: Insurance splits into two big families: **Life Insurance** and **Non-life (General) Insurance**. General insurance is then divided into many types such as health, travel, motor and property cover.

blocks.title: Which came first: Life or General?
blocks.phrase: Life before General, like L comes before G: LIC in 1956, GIC in 1972.
letters: Life Insurance Corporation of India – set up 1956
General Insurance Corporation of India – set up 1972
blocks.note: Both were created by Acts of Parliament after nationalisation; the 16-year gap is 1956 to 1972.

blocks.text: **Life insurance** is a financial cover for contingencies linked to human life: death, disability, accident, retirement and so on. Human life faces risks of death and disability from both natural and accidental causes. When a life is lost or a person is disabled, the household loses income, and life insurance acts as a hedge against that uncertain loss.

**Health insurance** covers medical expenses. Like every policy it is a contract between an insurer and an individual or group: the insurer agrees to provide a specified health cover at a particular premium, subject to the terms and conditions of the policy.

blocks.title: Where health sits
blocks.text: In India, health cover is part of non-life (general) insurance. It is sold by general insurers and also by 6 standalone health insurers that do only health business (count as per the 2024-25 book).

blocks.title: Life versus health in one glance
rows: Loss of household income when a life is lost or disabled
Contract between insurer and an individual or group

blocks.title: Main types of general insurance
rows: Domestic, overseas or both; protects you and family against travel accidents, sudden medical costs abroad, baggage or passport loss, flight interruptions or delays and late baggage.
Damage to the owner’s own vehicle plus third-party liability for injury or damage to another person’s life or property caused by the vehicle in a public place.
Buildings, machinery, stocks etc. against fire and allied perils, burglary and similar risks.
Goods in transit by sea, air, rail, road or courier.
The hulls of ships and boats.

blocks.title: Motor cover is compulsory
blocks.text: Driving a motor vehicle in a public place without insurance is a punishable offence, so cover is needed for as long as you own the vehicle. The law makes the owner liable for third-party injury or property damage, which is why third-party cover is the mandatory minimum.

blocks.title: Marine and aviation property covers
blocks.phrase: CHA: Cargo = goods on the move, Hull = the boat itself, Aviation = the aircraft.
letters: Marine Cargo – goods in transit by sea, air, rail, road, courier
Marine Hull – hulls of ships and boats

blocks.text: Property insurance is a vast category of general insurance. The cover on offer depends entirely on the kind of property the customer wants to protect.

sections.title: GIC Re and the four general insurers

blocks.text: General insurance in India was **nationalised in 1972**. In all, 107 insurers were merged into four companies: National, New India, Oriental and United India. The **General Insurance Corporation of India (GIC)** was incorporated in 1972 and those four companies became its subsidiaries.

blocks.title: GIC milestones
items: GIC incorporated; 107 insurers grouped into four companies, which become its subsidiaries.
Nov 2000
GIC notified as the Indian Reinsurer; its supervisory role over the subsidiaries ends.
March 2003
GIC stops being their holding company; ownership of the four insurers passes to the Government of India.

blocks.title: IRDAI at a glance
rows: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India
Regulator of the Indian insurance industry; protects policyholders’ interests and works for the orderly growth of the industry
Frames regulations under Section 114A of the Insurance Act, 1938

blocks.text: IRDAI closely monitors the insurance sector so that the industry grows in a healthy way and policyholders are protected. It is the regulator for all insurers, public or private, including the state-owned general insurers.

blocks.title: Insurance regulation and redress
items: Insurance Act, 1938
The parent law; Section 114A gives rule-making power
IRDAI (Hyderabad)

Insurers
LIC, GIC Re, general, health and private insurers
Insurance Ombudsman
Out-of-court redress for individual policyholders

blocks.text: The **Insurance Ombudsman scheme** was created by the Government of India so that individual policyholders can have complaints settled outside the courts in a cost-effective, efficient and impartial way. Any policyholder with a grievance against an insurer may complain to the Ombudsman for their location, either personally or through legal heirs, a nominee or an assignee.

blocks.title: D-SIIs
blocks.text: IRDAI has named three state-run insurers as Domestic Systemically Important Insurers (D-SIIs): LIC, GIC Re and New India Assurance. These are the insurers whose failure could shake the financial system.

blocks.title: The three D-SIIs
blocks.phrase: LGN – Life, General Re, New India: the big three that are too big to fail.
letters: General Insurance Corporation of India (GIC Re)
blocks.note: HDFC Life and ICICI Prudential are not D-SIIs.

blocks.text: At the time the book was written, **68 insurers** were operating in India. Counts change as licences are granted, so treat these as figures from the 2024-25 syllabus.

rows: 6 (the 4 PSU general insurers plus ECGC and AIC)
Re-insurers (incl. foreign branches and Lloyd’s India)

blocks.text: The two specialised public insurers are **ECGC** (export credit) and **AIC** (agriculture insurance). Together with LIC, the four general insurers and GIC Re, they make up the 8 public sector insurers.

blocks.title: Counting the insurers
blocks.phrase: Total 68 = 24 life + 27 general + 6 health + 11 re. Public 8 = 1 + 4 + 1 + 2; private 60 = 23 + 21 + 6 + 10.
letters: LIC (1), four PSU general insurers (4), GIC Re (1), ECGC and AIC (2)
blocks.note: Private general = 27 − 6 public = 21; private life = 24 − 1 = 23; private re = 11 − 1 = 10.

blocks.title: Market size (FY20 data in the book)
items: Government efforts to insure the uninsured have steadily lifted insurance penetration.
Gross direct premiums of non-life insurers reached US$ 20.33 billion in FY20 (up to December 2019).
Till February 2020 of FY20 they reached US$ 24.82 billion, a year-on-year growth of 14.03 %.
Overall insurance penetration (premiums as % of GDP) rose from 2.71 % in 2001 to 3.69 % in 2017.
In the same period private insurers grew premium collection by 17 %, against 9 % for state-owned non-life insurers.
Private sector share of the non-life market rose from 13.12 % in FY03 to 55.70 % in FY20.

blocks.title: Penetration, in plain words
blocks.text: Insurance penetration is premium income as a percentage of GDP. It tells you how deeply insurance has spread; a rise from 2.71 % to 3.69 % means it grew over 2001 to 2017.

The following reforms and proposals were described as recent developments in the 2024-25 book. Several were proposals at the time, so check current status before relying on them in an exam on latest affairs.

blocks.title: Reforms at a glance
rows: Invest up to 30 % of assets in BFSI
Insurers may deploy up to 30 % of assets in the banking, financial services and insurance sector for better investment income.
Proposal to reduce the ₹100 crore minimum capital for new insurers, enabling mono-line firms for motor, property, agri, SME, travel or consumer electronics.
IRDAI extended the procedure so insurers can launch products faster, pilot them in small groups and customise cover.
Proposed single window to track and file complaints, building trust between customers and insurers.
Lower premium based on kilometres driven, measured by a free telematics device.
Proposed regulator-supervised marketplace for standardisation, transparency, less mis-selling and fraud; supports OPD covers.
Proposed single licence to offer life, health and general cover under one roof.
A corporate agent (CA) can tie up with 9 insurers and an insurance marketing firm (IMF) with 6, for each of life, general and health.
Controlled testing of new products and technologies; maximum experimentation period of 36 months, with mid-way approval for faster go-live.

blocks.title: Tie-up limits and sandbox numbers
blocks.phrase: CA beats IMF, 9 to 6; sandbox is 3 years, 36 months.
letters: Corporate agent: up to 9 insurers per line of business
Insurance marketing firm: up to 6 insurers per line of business
Insurers may put up to 30 % of assets in the sector
blocks.note: Old tie-up limit was a third of the new one, which is why it is called a 3x increase.

blocks.title: Platform names
blocks.text: Bima Bharosa is the complaint-handling platform. Bima Sugam is the proposed one-stop marketplace for buying and servicing policies. Do not swap them in an exam.

**Bancassurance** means selling insurance and banking products through the same channel, most commonly through bank branches. In practice it is distributing insurance and other financial products through banks.

blocks.title: How bancassurance works in India
items: The RBI recognises bancassurance and lets a bank give physical space in selected branches to an insurer.
The insurer sells its products to the bank’s customers there, with adequate disclosure and transparency.
The bank earns referral fees, putting its existing resources and customer base to use.

blocks.title: RBI guidelines
items: Banks may act as brokers and sell policies of several insurance companies.
They can act as corporate agents without prior RBI approval.
To raise insurance penetration, banks may act as brokers, set up their own insurance subsidiaries and make referrals for multiple companies.

blocks.title: Old and new IRDAI norms
rows: Insurers it may tie up with
Only one life insurer and one non-life insurer

blocks.title: Bancassurance in one line
blocks.text: Bancassurance = insurance sold through banks. Under the older rule a bank-agent could sell for just one life and one non-life insurer; the new approach lets banks broker policies of many insurers.

**Para-banking** means financial services that banks offer beyond core deposits and lending: insurance business, underwriting, equipment leasing, mutual funds, pension fund management and similar activities. Banks usually do these through subsidiaries, which they are allowed to form under Section 19(1) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.

blocks.title: Extra facts that often come up
rows: Examples: SBI Pension Funds Pvt. Ltd, SBI Mutual Fund and ICICI Ventures.
A bank may set up a subsidiary or joint venture and also do insurance broking or agency.
Banks may enter this business under the framework of the PFRDA Act, 2013.
